column3: Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew names flock before herd and joins them with “and”.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says leaven shall not be seen with you.
The towns are described as your gates; an explicit noun for the animal is not added.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew uses the broader verb for cooking rather than explicitly specifying roasting.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew repeats counting seven weeks.
The Hebrew retains the gift of your hand and describes the blessing as prospective.
Son, daughter, male servant, female servant, and widow are each singular in the Hebrew; the LORD your God is named again in the choice of the place.
The Hebrew describes the addressee as a slave in the singular and separately joins keeping and doing the statutes.
The Hebrew says during your gathering, rather than explicitly after it.
Son, daughter, male servant, female servant, and widow are each singular in the Hebrew, and their location is described as your gates.
The Hebrew says you shall be only joyful and names the LORD again as choosing the place.
The Hebrew twice retains the LORD’s face and says to appear empty, without explicitly adding hands.
The Hebrew says each according to the gift of his hand, without explicitly repeating the command to appear.
The towns are called your gates in the Hebrew.
The Hebrew describes denying justice as bending judgment and partiality in terms of recognizing faces.
The Hebrew repeats justice, rather than explicitly adding “alone.”
The Hebrew uses the verb for planting.
The Hebrew addresses one person rather than saying “for yourselves.”
